new_concepts.name: optimal stopping problem
new_concepts.reminder: An optimal stopping problem asks for a stopping time that maximizes the expected reward of stopping a random process.
new_concepts.definition: Let $(Z_n)_{0\le n\le N}$, with $N\le\infty$, be integrable rewards adapted to a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$. The optimal stopping problem asks for the [expected value](c:expected-value) $V=\sup_\tau\mathbb{E}[Z_\tau]$ over all [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau\le N$, with $\tau<\infty$ almost surely when $N=\infty$, and for an optimal $\tau^*$ with $\mathbb{E}[Z_{\tau^*}]=V$. Because $\tau$ is a stopping time, each decision to stop uses only the information available at that time.

new_concepts.name: Snell envelope
new_concepts.reminder: The Snell envelope of a reward process is the smallest supermartingale that lies above it.
new_concepts.definition: Let $(Z_n)_{0\le n\le N}$ be an adapted process of integrable rewards for a filtration $(\mathcal{F}_n)$. Its Snell envelope is defined backwards by $U_N=Z_N$ and $U_n=\max(Z_n,\mathbb{E}[U_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n])$ for $n<N$. It is the smallest [supermartingale](c:supermartingale) with $U_n\ge Z_n$ for all $n$, and $U_n=\operatorname{ess\,sup}_\tau\mathbb{E}[Z_\tau\mid\mathcal{F}_n]$ over the [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau$ with $n\le\tau\le N$.

new_concepts.name: supermartingale
new_concepts.reminder: A supermartingale is an adapted integrable process whose conditional mean of the next value is at most the present value.
new_concepts.definition: An adapted process $(X_n)$ of [integrable](c:integrable-function) random variables for a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ is a supermartingale when the [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation) satisfies $\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]\le X_n$ almost surely for every $n$. In continuous time the condition is $\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]\le X_s$ for $s\le t$. So a supermartingale decreases on average, and $-X$ is a [submartingale](c:submartingale).

statement: For an adapted gain process $(G_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with $\mathbb{E}\sup_k |G_k| < \infty$, the [Snell envelope](c:snell-envelope) $S_n = \operatorname{ess\,sup}_{\tau \in \mathcal{M}_n} \mathbb{E}(G_\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_n)$ over finite [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau \ge n$ satisfies $S_n = \max(G_n, \mathbb{E}(S_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n))$ and $V_n = \mathbb{E} S_n$ for the [optimal stopping problem](c:optimal-stopping-problem), and it is the smallest [supermartingale](c:supermartingale) above $G$. If $\tau_n = \inf\{k \ge n : S_k = G_k\}$ is finite a.s., it is the smallest optimal time. Otherwise no optimal time exists.

hypotheses.text: The gain process $(G_n)_{n \ge 0}$ is adapted to a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \ge 0}$.
The gains satisfy $\mathbb{E}\sup_{k \ge 0}|G_k| < \infty$.

conclusion: $S_n = \max(G_n, \mathbb{E}(S_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n))$, $V_n = \mathbb{E} S_n$, $S$ is the smallest supermartingale above $G$, $(S_{k \wedge \tau_n})_{k \ge n}$ is a [martingale](c:martingale), every optimal $\tau^*$ satisfies $\tau_n \le \tau^*$, and $\tau_n$ is optimal if and only if $P(\tau_n < \infty) = 1$.

proofs.name: Essential supremum and monotone limits
proofs.slogan: Write the envelope as a monotone limit of conditional gains, then pass to infinite stopping times with integrable bounds.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for every $n \ge 0$.

roles.why: Adaptedness makes $G_n$ an admissible stopped gain at time $n$, so $S_n \ge G_n$, and it makes $\tau_n$ a [stopping time](c:stopping-time).
The integrable bound $G^* = \sup_k |G_k|$ gives $|S_n| \le \mathbb{E}(G^* \mid \mathcal{F}_n)$ and controls every limit of stopped values.

steps.slogan: Define the envelope as an [essential supremum](c:essential-supremum) and bound it by $\mathbb{E}(G^* \mid \mathcal{F}_n)$.
steps.detail: The [essential supremum](c:essential-supremum) is the supremum of a countable subfamily, so $S_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable, and $G_n \le S_n \le \mathbb{E}(G^* \mid \mathcal{F}_n)$ because every conditional gain lies in $[-\mathbb{E}(G^* \mid \mathcal{F}_n), \mathbb{E}(G^* \mid \mathcal{F}_n)]$.

steps.slogan: Show that the conditional gains form an upward directed family, so the envelope is an increasing limit.
steps.detail: Pasting $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ on the event where the first conditional gain is larger gives a stopping time with the larger conditional gain, so $S_m = \lim_j \mathbb{E}(G_{\rho_j} \mid \mathcal{F}_m)$ increasingly, and monotone convergence gives $V_m = \mathbb{E} S_m$.

steps.slogan: Derive the recurrence $S_n = \max(G_n, \mathbb{E}(S_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n))$ from both sides.
steps.detail: Conditional monotone convergence along the increasing sequence gives $\mathbb{E}(S_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n) \le S_n$, and splitting $\tau$ on $\{\tau = n\}$ with the tower property gives the reverse bound, so $S$ is a [supermartingale](c:supermartingale) above $G$.

steps.slogan: Show that the stopped envelope is a [martingale](c:martingale) and that stopped values converge in $L^1$.
steps.detail: Before $\tau_n$ the envelope satisfies $S_k = \mathbb{E}(S_{k+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_k)$, and for an a.s. finite $\sigma$ the bound $\mathbb{E}|S_{\sigma \wedge m} - S_\sigma| \le 2\mathbb{E}(1\{\sigma > m\} G^*)$ tends to $0$ by dominated convergence.

steps.slogan: Use Fatou's lemma to show that every supermartingale above the gain lies above the envelope.
steps.detail: For a [supermartingale](c:supermartingale) $\tilde S \ge G$, optional sampling at $\tau \wedge m$ and the conditional Fatou lemma with the lower bound $-G^*$ give $\mathbb{E}(G_\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_k) \le \mathbb{E}(\tilde S_\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_k) \le \tilde S_k$, so $S_k \le \tilde S_k$.

steps.slogan: Show that optimal times stop where the envelope meets the gain, and that $\tau_n$ is optimal when finite.
steps.detail: For an optimal $\tau^*$, $\mathbb{E} G_{\tau^*} \le \mathbb{E} S_{\tau^*} \le \mathbb{E} S_n = V_n$ forces $S_{\tau^*} = G_{\tau^*}$, so $\tau_n \le \tau^*$. If $\tau_n < \infty$ a.s., the $L^1$ limit gives $S_n = \mathbb{E}(G_{\tau_n} \mid \mathcal{F}_n)$.

concepts.c:supermartingale: The envelope is the smallest supermartingale that dominates the gain.
concepts.c:essential-supremum: The essential supremum makes the supremum of uncountably many conditional gains a well-defined random variable.

statement: If $n \ge 2$ applicants arrive in a uniformly random order ([permutation](c:permutation)) and each decision may use only relative ranks, then the best rule for choosing the best applicant rejects the first $s_n - 1$ applicants and accepts the next applicant who is better than all earlier ones. Here $s_n$ is the largest $s \ge 2$ with $\sum_{j=s-1}^{n-1} 1/j \ge 1$. The success probability is $V_n = \frac{s_n - 1}{n} \sum_{j=s_n-1}^{n-1} \frac1j$, and $s_n/n \to 1/e$ and $V_n \to 1/e$. This solves an [optimal stopping problem](c:optimal-stopping-problem).

hypotheses.text: All $n!$ orders of the applicants are equally likely, so the order is a uniform random [permutation](c:permutation).
Each decision is a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) of the relative ranks seen so far, and rejected applicants cannot be recalled.

conclusion: The threshold rule with threshold $s_n$ is optimal, it succeeds with probability $V_n = \frac{s_n-1}{n}\sum_{j=s_n-1}^{n-1} \frac1j$, and both $s_n/n$ and $V_n$ tend to $1/e$.

proofs.name: Reduction to the odds theorem
proofs.slogan: Relative ranks are independent, so choosing the best applicant means stopping on the last record, which the odds theorem solves.
proofs.scope: The full statement, including both limits.

roles.why: A uniform order makes the relative ranks [independent](c:independent-random-variables), with $P(\text{applicant } k \text{ is a record}) = 1/k$.
Rules that use only relative ranks are exactly the stopping times of the filtration that the odds theorem allows.

steps.slogan: Show that the relative ranks are independent and uniform with a bijection.
steps.detail: The map from orders to sequences $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ with $1 \le X_k \le k$ is injective, and both sets have $n!$ elements, so a uniform [permutation](c:permutation) gives independent uniform $X_k$.

steps.slogan: Show that choosing the best applicant means stopping on the last record.
steps.detail: With $I_k = 1\{X_k = 1\}$, applicant $\tau$ is the overall best exactly when $I_\tau = 1$ and $I_j = 0$ for all $j > \tau$, and the future indicators are independent of the past ranks.

steps.slogan: Apply the odds theorem with the odds $r_k = 1/(k-1)$.
steps.detail: The tail sums are $R_l = \sum_{j=l-1}^{n-1} 1/j$, so the threshold of the odds theorem is $s_n$, and the rule that waits until $s_n$ and takes the first record is optimal.

steps.slogan: Compute the success probability with a telescoping product.
steps.detail: The odds theorem gives $V_n = \prod_{j \ge s_n} q_j \cdot R_{s_n}$, and $\prod_{j=s}^n (j-1)/j = (s-1)/n$ telescopes.

steps.slogan: Compare the [harmonic sums](c:harmonic-series) with logarithms to get the limits $1/e$.
steps.detail: Integral bounds give $n/e < s_n \le (n-1)/e + 2$ and $(s_n - 1)/n \le V_n \le s_n/n$, and both bounds tend to $1/e$.

new_concepts.name: optimal stopping problem
new_concepts.reminder: An optimal stopping problem asks for a stopping time that maximizes the expected reward of stopping a random process.
new_concepts.definition: Let $(Z_n)_{0\le n\le N}$, with $N\le\infty$, be integrable rewards adapted to a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$. The optimal stopping problem asks for the [expected value](c:expected-value) $V=\sup_\tau\mathbb{E}[Z_\tau]$ over all [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau\le N$, with $\tau<\infty$ almost surely when $N=\infty$, and for an optimal $\tau^*$ with $\mathbb{E}[Z_{\tau^*}]=V$. Because $\tau$ is a stopping time, each decision to stop uses only the information available at that time.

statement: For [independent](c:independent-random-variables) [indicators](c:bernoulli-distribution) $I_1, \dots, I_n$ with odds $r_j = p_j/(1-p_j)$, let $s = \max(\{1\} \cup \{l : \sum_{j=l}^n r_j \ge 1\})$. In the [optimal stopping problem](c:optimal-stopping-problem) of stopping on the last success, the [stopping time](c:stopping-time) that waits until index $s$ and then stops at the first success is optimal. Its win probability is the probability of exactly one success among $I_s, \dots, I_n$, which is $\prod_{j=s}^n q_j \sum_{j=s}^n r_j$ when every $p_j < 1$ for $j \ge s$.

hypotheses.text: The indicators $I_1, \dots, I_n$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) with known success probabilities $p_j$.
For every $k$, $I_k$ is $\mathcal{F}_k$-measurable and $(I_{k+1}, \dots, I_n)$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_k$ for the [filtration](c:filtration) of the decision maker.

conclusion: The threshold rule $\tau_s$ maximizes $P(I_\tau = 1, I_{\tau+1} = \dots = I_n = 0)$, and the maximum equals $\sum_{k=s}^n p_k \prod_{j \ne k} q_j$, which is $\prod_{j=s}^n q_j \sum_{j=s}^n r_j$ when all these $q_j > 0$.

proofs.name: Backward induction on the Snell envelope
proofs.slogan: Turn the win probability into a gain process, then compute its Snell envelope backward and read off the threshold.
proofs.scope: The full theorem, including indices with $p_j = 1$.

roles.why: Independence makes the continuation values numbers, not random variables, and gives the probability of exactly one success.
Independence of the future from the information at time $k$ turns the win probability into $\mathbb{E} G_\tau$ and makes the envelope recursion explicit.

steps.slogan: Write the win probability as the expected gain $\mathbb{E} G_\tau$ with $G_k = I_k Q_{k+1}$.
steps.detail: Since $(I_{k+1}, \dots, I_n)$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_k$, the probability that a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau$ wins is $\sum_k \mathbb{E}(1\{\tau = k\} I_k) Q_{k+1}$ with $Q_m = \prod_{j \ge m} q_j$.

steps.slogan: Show that the [Snell envelope](c:snell-envelope) is $\max(I_k Q_{k+1}, c_k)$ with numbers $c_k$.
steps.detail: Backward induction: if $S_k$ is a function of $I_k$ alone, then $\mathbb{E}(S_k \mid \mathcal{F}_{k-1}) = \mathbb{E} S_k$ is a number $c_{k-1} = p_k \max(Q_{k+1}, c_k) + q_k c_k$.

steps.slogan: Compare the probability $f(l)$ of exactly one later success with the probability $Q_l$ of none.
steps.detail: The recursion $f(m) = p_m Q_{m+1} + q_m f(m+1)$ holds, and for $l > s$ all odds are finite, so $f(l) = Q_l R_l < Q_l$ because $R_l < 1$.

steps.slogan: Show by backward induction that the continuation value after index $k \ge s$ is $f(k+1)$.
steps.detail: If $c_k = f(k+1) \le Q_{k+1}$, then $c_{k-1} = p_k Q_{k+1} + q_k f(k+1) = f(k)$, so from $s$ on the envelope equals the gain at every success.

steps.slogan: Show that before index $s$ continuing is always at least as good as stopping.
steps.detail: If $s \ge 2$ then $R_s \ge 1$, so $Q_{k+1} \le Q_s \le f(s)$ for $k < s$, the envelope is the constant $f(s)$ before $s$, and $\mathbb{E} S_1 = f(s)$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the threshold rule attains the value $f(s)$ and is therefore optimal.
steps.detail: The finite-horizon theorem gives the optimal value $\mathbb{E} S_1 = f(s)$, and $\tau_s$ wins exactly when $I_s, \dots, I_n$ contain one success, which has probability $f(s)$.

concepts.c:bernoulli-distribution: Each observation is a Bernoulli indicator of success with known parameter.
concepts.c:optimal-stopping-problem: Stopping on the last success is a finite-horizon optimal stopping problem.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The decision to stop at index k may use only the information up to k.

proofs.name: Iterative method
proofs.slogan: Build the smallest excessive majorant as $\lim Q^n G$, then trap the value between a [supermartingale](c:supermartingale) bound and a [martingale](c:martingale) construction.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem: the iteration, the Wald-Bellman equation and the minimality. It does not treat the existence of an optimal stopping time.

roles.why: The Markov property turns $\mathbb{E}_x[F(X_{n+1}) \mid \mathcal{F}_n]$ into $TF(X_n)$.
The integrable bound keeps every iterate finite and justifies the limits.
A finite stopping time lets $G(X_{\tau \wedge k})$ converge to $G(X_\tau)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the iterates $Q^n G$ increase and stay below an integrable bound.
steps.detail: With $H(x) = \mathbb{E}_x \sup_n |G(X_n)|$, induction and the Markov property give $G \le Q^n G \le Q^{n+1} G$ and $|Q^n G| \le H$. Call the limit $U$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit in $Q^{n+1}G = \max(G, TQ^nG)$ by monotone convergence.
steps.detail: Monotone convergence with the integrable lower bound $-H(X_1)$ gives $TQ^nG \to TU$, so $U = \max(G, TU)$. Thus $U$ is an [excessive function](c:excessive-function) above $G$.

steps.slogan: Every excessive majorant $F$ of $G$ lies above every iterate $Q^n G$.
steps.detail: From $F \ge G$ and $TF \le F$ we get $QF \le F$. The operator $Q$ is monotone, so induction gives $Q^n G \le F$ for all $n$, and hence $U \le F$.

steps.slogan: Bound every stopping gain by $U$ with the [supermartingale](c:supermartingale) $U(X_n)$.
steps.detail: Since $TU \le U$, $U(X_n)$ is a supermartingale. Optional stopping at $\tau \wedge k$ gives $\mathbb{E}_x G(X_{\tau\wedge k}) \le U(x)$, and dominated convergence as $k \to \infty$ gives $V \le U$.

steps.slogan: Attain $Q^n G$ with the first time the finite-horizon value meets the gain.
steps.detail: The process $Y_k = Q^{n-k}G(X_k)$ is a [martingale](c:martingale) up to $\tau_n = \min\{k : Y_k = G(X_k)\}$, because $Y_k = TQ^{n-k-1}G(X_k)$ before $\tau_n$. So $\mathbb{E}_x G(X_{\tau_n}) = Q^nG(x)$ and $V \ge U$.

steps.slogan: Identify the value with the smallest excessive majorant $U$.
steps.detail: The two bounds give $V = U = \lim Q^n G$. The limit equation gives $V = \max(G, TV)$, and the minimality step gives $F \ge V$ for every excessive majorant $F$ of $G$.

new_concepts.name: excessive function
new_concepts.reminder: An excessive function for a Markov kernel $P$ is a nonnegative function with $Pf\le f$.
new_concepts.definition: Let $P$ be a [Markov kernel](c:markov-kernel) on a measurable space $S$. A measurable function $f:S\to[0,\infty]$ is excessive (or $P$-superharmonic) when $Pf(x)=\int f(y)\,P(x,dy)\le f(x)$ for every $x\in S$. For a continuous-time Markov semigroup $(P_t)$, a measurable $f\ge0$ is excessive when $P_tf\le f$ for all $t\ge0$ and $P_tf\to f$ pointwise as $t\to0$.

new_concepts.name: optimal stopping problem
new_concepts.reminder: An optimal stopping problem asks for a stopping time that maximizes the expected reward of stopping a random process.
new_concepts.definition: Let $(Z_n)_{0\le n\le N}$, with $N\le\infty$, be integrable rewards adapted to a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$. The optimal stopping problem asks for the [expected value](c:expected-value) $V=\sup_\tau\mathbb{E}[Z_\tau]$ over all [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau\le N$, with $\tau<\infty$ almost surely when $N=\infty$, and for an optimal $\tau^*$ with $\mathbb{E}[Z_{\tau^*}]=V$. Because $\tau$ is a stopping time, each decision to stop uses only the information available at that time.

new_concepts.name: supermartingale
new_concepts.reminder: A supermartingale is an adapted integrable process whose conditional mean of the next value is at most the present value.
new_concepts.definition: An adapted process $(X_n)$ of [integrable](c:integrable-function) random variables for a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ is a supermartingale when the [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation) satisfies $\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]\le X_n$ almost surely for every $n$. In continuous time the condition is $\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]\le X_s$ for $s\le t$. So a supermartingale decreases on average, and $-X$ is a [submartingale](c:submartingale).

statement: Let $X$ solve the [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) $dX_t = b(X_t)\,dt + \sigma(X_t)\,dW_t$ in an open interval $I$. Let $V$ be a [continuously differentiable](c:continuously-differentiable-map) function on $I$ that is $C^2$ off a finite set $F$ where $\sigma \ne 0$, and that solves $\min\{\mathcal L V - \lambda V + w,\ z - V\} = 0$ off $F$. Then the exit time $\tau^*$ of $X$ from $D = \{V < z\}$ minimizes $J[\tau] = E[\int_0^\tau e^{-\lambda s} w(X_s)\,ds + e^{-\lambda\tau} z(X_\tau)]$ over the finite [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau$ for which the [Itô integral](c:ito-integral) $\int_0^\tau e^{-\lambda s} V'(X_s)\sigma(X_s)\,dW_s$ has mean zero, if $\tau^*$ is one of them and $E|V(X_0)| < \infty$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a continuous solution of $dX_t = b(X_t)\,dt + \sigma(X_t)\,dW_t$ that stays in the open interval $I$, with $b$ and $\sigma$ continuous.
$V$ is $C^1$ on $I$ and $C^2$ on $I \setminus F$ for a finite set $F$, $V''$ is bounded near $F$, and $\sigma \ne 0$ on $F$.
$\min\{\mathcal L V - \lambda V + w,\ z - V\} = 0$ on $I \setminus F$, with $w$ and $z$ continuous and $\lambda \ge 0$.
$E|V(X_0)| < \infty$, and $\tau^*$ is a.s. finite with $E\int_0^{\tau^*} e^{-\lambda s} V'(X_s)\sigma(X_s)\,dW_s = 0$.

conclusion: $J[\tau^*] = E\,V(X_0) \le J[\tau]$ for every admissible $\tau$, so $E\,V(X_0)$ is the optimal cost and $V$ is the [value function](c:value-function) of the problem.

proofs.name: Relaxed Itô rule and comparison
proofs.slogan: Extend Itô's rule to the $C^1$ function $V$, then compare its expansion with the cost of any rule for the [optimal stopping problem](c:optimal-stopping-problem).
proofs.scope: The full statement. The Itô rule is proved for finitely many points where $V$ is only $C^1$, not for a general measurable second derivative.

roles.why: The equation and the continuity of the coefficients give Itô's formula and the bounds after localization.
A $C^1$ function with a bounded second derivative off $F$ is a limit of $C^2$ functions, and $\sigma \ne 0$ on $F$ makes the time at $F$ negligible.
The two inequalities give the lower bound, and the equation inside $D$ gives the equality for $\tau^*$.
A mean-zero stochastic integral and an integrable $V(X_0)$ make the expansion of $V$ have mean $E\,V(X_0)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the diffusion spends zero time at each point where $\sigma \ne 0$.
steps.detail: Itô's formula for $F_\varepsilon$ with $F_\varepsilon'' = g_\varepsilon \ge 1_{\{a\}}$ and $|F_\varepsilon'| \le 4\varepsilon$ bounds $\tfrac12\sigma(a)^2$ times the [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) of $\{s \le t : X_s = a\}$ by terms that tend to zero.

steps.slogan: Approximate $V$ by $C^2$ functions whose second derivatives equal $V''$ away from $F$.
steps.detail: Replace $V''$ by a linear interpolation on $[a - 1/n, a + 1/n]$ for each $a \in F$ and integrate twice. The approximations converge to $V$ with their first derivatives, uniformly on compact sets.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit in Itô's formula for the approximations to get Itô's rule for $V$.
steps.detail: The second-derivative terms converge at almost every time because the time spent at $F$ is null, and the stochastic integrals converge in $L^2$ by the Itô isometry.

steps.slogan: Bound the cost of every admissible rule below by the mean of $V(X_0)$.
steps.detail: The expansion $Y_\tau = V(X_0) + M_\tau$ has mean $E\,V(X_0)$, and $V \le z$ and $\lambda V - \mathcal L V \le w$ give $Y_\tau \le Z_\tau$, the realized cost of $\tau$.

steps.slogan: Show that the exit rule from the continuation region turns both bounds into equalities.
steps.detail: Before $\tau^*$ the process is in $D$, where $\mathcal L V - \lambda V + w = 0$, and at $\tau^*$ it is in the closed set $\{V = z\}$, so $Y_{\tau^*} = Z_{\tau^*}$.

concepts.c:stochastic-differential-equation: The state of the stopping problem is the solution of a one-dimensional stochastic differential equation.
concepts.c:continuously-differentiable-map: Smooth fit means that V is continuously differentiable across the boundary of the continuation region.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The controller chooses a stopping time, and the theorem compares all admissible stopping times.
concepts.c:ito-integral: The mean-zero condition on the Itô integral defines the admissible class of stopping times.
concepts.c:value-function: The theorem identifies the solution of the variational inequality with the value function.
concepts.c:optimal-stopping-problem: The cost J is the objective of an optimal stopping problem for a diffusion.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: The time spent at the points of F has Lebesgue measure zero, so V'' is not needed there.

source.ref: R. van Handel, Stochastic Calculus, Filtering, and Stochastic Control (ACM 217 lecture notes, 2007), Proposition 8.1.3 and its proof, p. 210, with Proposition 8.1.5 on pp. 210-211.

statement: In the Black-Scholes model with $r > 0$, the perpetual American put has price $V(x) = K - x$ for $x \le L^*$ and $V(x) = (K - L^*)(x/L^*)^{-2r/\sigma^2}$ for $x \ge L^*$, where $L^* = 2rK/(2r + \sigma^2)$. The first [stopping time](c:stopping-time) at which the price reaches $L^*$ is optimal for this [optimal stopping problem](c:optimal-stopping-problem).

hypotheses.text: The interest rate $r$, the volatility $\sigma$ and the strike $K$ are strictly positive.
Under $P^*$, $S_t = x\exp(\sigma B_t + (r - \sigma^2/2)t)$ with a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$.
Exercise at a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau$ pays $(K - S_\tau)^+$ at time $\tau$, and no exercise pays $0$.

conclusion: $\sup_\tau \mathbb{E}^*[e^{-r\tau}(K - S_\tau)^+] = V(x)$ for every $x > 0$, and $\tau^* = \inf\{t : S_t \le L^*\}$ attains it.

proofs.name: Verification of the smooth-fit candidate
proofs.slogan: Show that the discounted candidate is a [supermartingale](c:supermartingale) above the payoff, and that it is a [martingale](c:martingale) until the price first reaches $L^*$.
proofs.scope: The value for every initial price and the optimality of $\tau^*$, for $r > 0$. The case $r = 0$ is excluded.

roles.why: Positive rates make $\gamma > 0$ and $L^* < K$, and the discount factor kills the payoff at $\tau = \infty$.
The model gives the generator for Itô's formula and the exponential martingale $e^{-rt}S_t^{-\gamma}$.
The payoff convention fixes the gain that the supermartingale bound must dominate.

steps.slogan: Check that the candidate $V$ is $C^1$, [convex](c:convex-function) and above the payoff.
steps.detail: Both branches have slope $-1$ at $L^*$, which is smooth fit. Convexity puts $V$ above its tangent $K - x$. The generator gives $-rK$ below $L^*$ and $0$ above $L^*$.

steps.slogan: Prove that $e^{-rt}V(S_t)$ is a [supermartingale](c:supermartingale) with Itô's formula after mollification.
steps.detail: In log coordinates the candidate has a Lipschitz derivative. A [mollifier](c:mollifier) gives smooth functions with nonpositive generator. Itô's formula and the martingale property of the stochastic integral give supermartingales, and the uniform limit keeps the property.

steps.slogan: Bound the discounted payoff of every exercise rule by $V(x)$ with optional stopping.
steps.detail: Optional stopping at $\tau \wedge t$ and dominated convergence as $t \to \infty$ give $\mathbb{E}^*[e^{-r\tau}V(S_\tau)] \le V(x)$. The payoff is at most $V$.

steps.slogan: Compute the payoff of $\tau^*$ with the exponential [martingale](c:martingale) $e^{-rt}S_t^{-\gamma}$.
steps.detail: Stopped at $\tau^*$ this martingale is bounded by $(L^*)^{-\gamma}$. Optional stopping and dominated convergence give $\mathbb{E}^*[e^{-r\tau^*}] = (x/L^*)^{-\gamma}$, so $\tau^*$ pays $V(x)$.

steps.slogan: Join the two bounds to identify the value of the [optimal stopping problem](c:optimal-stopping-problem).
steps.detail: The upper bound holds for every stopping time and $\tau^*$ attains it. So the price is $V(x)$ and $\tau^*$ is an optimal exercise rule.

concepts.c:stopping-time: Exercise rules are stopping times, and the optimal one is a hitting time.
concepts.c:optimal-stopping-problem: The option price is the value of an optimal stopping problem with discounting.
concepts.c:brownian-motion: The asset price is the exponential of a Brownian motion with drift.
concepts.c:supermartingale: The discounted candidate value is a supermartingale, which bounds every exercise rule.
concepts.c:martingale: The exponential martingale of the price computes the discounted payoff of the hitting time.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity of the candidate puts it above the payoff line K minus x.
concepts.c:mollifier: Mollification smooths the candidate so that Itô's formula applies at the exercise boundary.
